easy.prompt: A network is called synchronous when which timing property holds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Message delays and process step times have known finite upper bounds.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Message delays are unbounded and unpredictable.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All nodes share one perfectly synchronized wall clock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No process ever crashes or drops a message.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what a 'known upper bound' lets a timeout designer safely choose.
easy.explanation: Synchrony means you can set a timeout that no correct execution ever exceeds.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With a known bound D, any reply arriving after D means the peer is faulty or the bound was wrong. Step 2: A client waiting past D can therefore treat silence as evidence. Step 3: That is why synchronous algorithms may use timeouts as failure evidence while async ones cannot.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the asynchronous model, the opposite of synchronous.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clock synchronization is separate; synchrony is about delay bounds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Failure behavior is a separate fault model, not a timing property.

easy.prompt: In the asynchronous model, what is assumed about message delays and processing speeds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The network guarantees FIFO order on every link.

choices.label: B
choices.body: There is no finite bound; a message or step may take arbitrarily long.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every message arrives within 1 millisecond.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Processes execute in strict lockstep rounds.

easy.hint: Next step: think about what 'no bound' implies for telling a slow node from a dead one.
easy.explanation: Asynchrony means any finite wait may still end with a late-but-correct reply.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: A node silent for 10 s might be crashed or just slow. Step 2: No timeout can separate the two cases in all executions. Step 3: This indistinguishability is the root of the FLP impossibility result.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Ordering is a separate channel property, not a timing bound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A fixed 1 ms bound is a synchronous assumption, not asynchrony.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lockstep rounds assume synchrony; async processes run at unrelated speeds.

easy.prompt: Under the crash-stop failure model, a faulty process does what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Halts permanently and sends nothing further, never emitting wrong messages.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sends malicious messages to different peers forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Keeps running while silently corrupting its disk.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Never fails under any circumstance.

easy.hint: Next step: separate 'stops' from 'lies'.
easy.explanation: Crash-stop faults are silent halts; survivors only observe missing future messages.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Node N crashes mid-broadcast: some peers got its last message, others did not. Step 2: N never equivocates—nobody receives a fabricated message from N. Step 3: Recovery therefore needs failover, not lie detection.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is Byzantine behavior, not crash-stop.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Crash-stop halts; ongoing corruption is a different fault class.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The model explicitly allows halting failures.

easy.prompt: An omission failure means what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A process skips some sends or receives—dropping messages—while otherwise following its program.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The process halts forever and never resumes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The process sends deliberately malicious lies.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The process runs with zero network delay.

easy.hint: Next step: think 'lost mail', not 'dead sender'.
easy.explanation: Omission is message loss by an otherwise correct process.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Sender transmits m1, m2, m3; only m1 and m3 arrive. Step 2: No fabricated message appears and the sender keeps running. Step 3: Retries and acknowledgments—not lie detection—are the matching remedy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Permanent halting is crash-stop, not omission.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Malicious content is Byzantine behavior, not omission.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Timing speed is unrelated to message loss.

easy.prompt: A Byzantine-faulty node may do what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only halt silently and stay silent.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only drop packets while otherwise obeying its program.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only run slowly during peak load.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deviate arbitrarily, including sending conflicting messages to different peers.

easy.hint: Next step: think 'traitor', not 'corpse'.
easy.explanation: Byzantine covers crashes, omissions, and malicious equivocation together.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Faulty general G tells A 'attack' and B 'retreat'. Step 2: Both A and B believe they heard the true order. Step 3: Agreement now needs lie-tolerant protocols (3f+1 replicas, signed evidence), not just failover.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Silent halting is crash-stop behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Benign loss is omission, a strict subset of Byzantine.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Slowness is a performance issue, not arbitrary deviation.

easy.prompt: The FLP impossibility result says what about deterministic consensus in a fully asynchronous system?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Consensus is trivial even with one crash.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Randomized algorithms are also impossible.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Synchronous systems are equally impossible.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No deterministic algorithm guarantees agreement, validity, and termination when even one crash is possible.

easy.hint: Next step: focus on the triple 'deterministic + async + one crash'.
easy.explanation: Asynchrony plus one fault admits an execution that never decides.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Start from a bivalent state where both 0 and 1 outcomes remain reachable. Step 2: The adversary delays the critical message or crashes its sender, keeping the system bivalent. Step 3: Hence real systems add timeouts, randomness, or partial synchrony to escape FLP.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: FLP proves the opposite: one crash suffices to break termination.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Randomization is a known escape route around FLP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: With timing bounds, consensus becomes solvable.

easy.prompt: When a heartbeat timeout expires in an asynchronous system, what may you conclude?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The peer is proven crashed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The peer is proven Byzantine.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The network partition has healed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only that the peer is suspected—possibly slow or partitioned, not proven crashed.

easy.hint: Next step: replace the word 'detected' with 'suspected'.
easy.explanation: Timeouts are hints in async systems, never proof.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Monitor misses two heartbeats from S and suspects it. Step 2: S is actually alive behind a congested link and keeps serving writes. Step 3: Acting as if S were dead causes split-brain—suspicion must trigger verification, not certainty.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Expiry is suspicion, never proof, under asynchrony.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Timeouts carry no evidence about malicious intent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Silence gives no information about healing.

easy.prompt: What does a Lamport timestamp give you?

choices.label: A
choices.body: True UTC time accurate to microseconds everywhere.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Proof that no messages were lost.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A total order of every event in the system.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A partial order consistent with happened-before: if A caused B, then clock(A) < clock(B).

easy.hint: Next step: remember the direction—causality implies clock order, not the reverse.
easy.explanation: Lamport clocks preserve causal direction, but concurrent events may take any stamp order.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Send event s at clock 4; receive event r computes max-plus-one to 5. Step 2: Every causal chain increments at each hop, so clocks rise along it. Step 3: But clock(A) < clock(B) alone does not prove A caused B—vector clocks are needed for that.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That needs physical clock sync, not Lamport clocks alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Timestamps do not detect packet loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Concurrent events are unordered; Lamport gives a partial order.

easy.prompt: In a vector clock, what does entry V_P[Q] represent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The GPS latitude of process Q.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The TCP port clients must use for Q.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The disk usage of process Q.

choices.label: D
choices.body: How many events of process Q have causally reached P—P's knowledge of Q's progress.

easy.hint: Next step: read the vector as 'what P has heard so far'.
easy.explanation: Each entry counts known events per process, enabling causality comparison.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: P holds [3,1,0]: it has seen 3 of its own events, 1 from Q, none from R. Step 2: When a message from Q carrying [2,4,1] arrives, P merges element-wise max. Step 3: P's new vector reflects everything causally before that message.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Location is unrelated to vector-clock semantics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ports are networking details, not causal history.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Storage metrics do not implement happened-before.

easy.prompt: What does at-least-once RPC delivery guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The call is delivered one or more times; duplicates are possible but loss is not.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The call is delivered exactly one time, never duplicated.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The call may be silently dropped with no retry.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Calls arrive in global causal order automatically.

easy.hint: Next step: split the guarantee into 'no loss' plus 'duplicates allowed'.
easy.explanation: At-least-once retries until an ack arrives, so redeliveries can duplicate side effects.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends charge($10), gets no ack due to a dropped reply. Step 2: It retries; the server executes charge a second time. Step 3: The customer is billed twice—at-least-once needs idempotent handlers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Exactly-once is stronger; at-least-once permits duplicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping without delivery is at-most-once behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ordering is a separate guarantee, not a delivery count.

easy.prompt: What does at-most-once RPC delivery guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lost calls are retried until acknowledged.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The call executes zero or one times; it is never duplicated, but it may be lost.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The call always executes at least one time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The call executes exactly once under all failures.

easy.hint: Next step: split the guarantee into 'no duplicates' plus 'loss allowed'.
easy.explanation: At-most-once sends without retrying, so crashes can lose the call silently.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client fires a notify() and its packet is dropped. Step 2: With no retry, the server never runs it—acceptable for idempotent-loss-tolerant pings. Step 3: For a payment, this silence would be wrong; you would want at-least-once plus dedup.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Retrying would risk duplicates, which at-most-once forbids.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is at-least-once; at-most-once may deliver zero times.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Exactly-once needs dedup machinery beyond fire-and-forget.

easy.prompt: An operation is idempotent when which property holds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Repeating it with the same arguments leaves the same final state as doing it once.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Repeating it is forbidden by the protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It always returns random data on retry.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It deletes the database on second execution.

easy.hint: Next step: test f(f(x)) == f(x) with a concrete example.
easy.explanation: SET key=5 twice still leaves 5; INCR twice does not.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: SET balance=100 runs twice: state stays 100 either way. Step 2: ADD 10 runs twice: 100 becomes 120, not 110—not idempotent. Step 3: So retries are safe for SET but dangerous for ADD without dedup.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Idempotence is about safe repetition, not forbidding it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Nondeterministic results are the opposite of idempotent stability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A destructive second run violates idempotence.

easy.prompt: A client gets a timeout with no response. Why is blindly retrying a non-idempotent call unsafe?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The first attempt may have executed; a retry could apply the effect twice.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Timeouts prove the server never ran the call.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Retries are forbidden in every distributed system.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Timeouts only happen when disks are full.

easy.hint: Next step: list the two possible worlds: executed vs lost.
easy.explanation: Timeout ambiguity means the caller cannot distinguish success from failure.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends debit($50); server executes it but the reply is dropped. Step 2: Client sees a timeout and retries. Step 3: Without dedup the account loses $100 for one intended debit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Timeouts prove nothing—the reply may simply be delayed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Retries are routine; they must be made safe, not banned.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Timeouts come from congestion, GC, partitions, or crashes.

easy.prompt: How does server-side deduplication with client request IDs make retries safe?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The server records each completed request ID and replays the stored result instead of re-executing duplicates.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The server ignores all retries without tracking anything.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The client encrypts retries so they cannot duplicate.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The server disables all retries network-wide.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what the server looks up when ID=42 arrives twice.
easy.explanation: A dedup table turns the second arrival into a cached replay.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: pay(id=42) executes; server stores (42 -> receipt). Step 2: Retry pay(id=42) arrives after the lost ack. Step 3: Server returns the stored receipt without touching the ledger.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Blind ignoring can drop legitimate first attempts too.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Encryption hides content; it does not detect repeats.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Dedup embraces retries and neutralizes them instead.

easy.prompt: TCP gives reliable ordered byte delivery on a connection. Why does that NOT equal exactly-once execution for applications?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Connections can break and clients retry, so the app may submit the same logical call twice over different connections.

choices.label: B
choices.body: TCP never retransmits lost segments.

choices.label: C
choices.body: TCP delivers bytes in random order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: TCP encrypts payloads against the application.

easy.hint: Next step: separate 'bytes arrived once per connection' from 'call ran once'.
easy.explanation: TCP's guarantee ends at the connection; app-level retries span connections.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends transfer(); server runs it, then the connection breaks before the ack. Step 2: TCP cannot report the outcome; the client opens a new connection and retries. Step 3: The server sees a second transfer()—only request IDs plus dedup stop the double debit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TCP does retransmit—that is precisely why bytes arrive reliably per connection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TCP delivers ordered bytes; the gap is at the application layer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Encryption is TLS's job and is unrelated to execution count.

easy.prompt: What is backpressure in an RPC system?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A firewall that blocks all RPC traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A cache that answers every request instantly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A faster network cable upgrade.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A signal from an overloaded receiver that slows senders, keeping queues bounded instead of dropping or OOMing.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what the receiver tells senders when its queue fills.
easy.explanation: Slow-down signals propagate overload to the edge instead of collapsing the core.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Server queue hits its limit and returns 429/retry-after. Step 2: Clients back off instead of piling on. Step 3: The queue drains and recovers rather than crashing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Backpressure throttles, it does not blackhole everything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Caching hides latency; backpressure controls send rate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hardware helps capacity but provides no overload signal.

easy.prompt: What is an RPC deadline (timeout budget)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A guarantee the server finishes in that time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A disk quota for request logs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Proof the call never executed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A bound on how long the caller waits before abandoning the call and treating it as failed.

easy.hint: Next step: ask whose waiting the deadline limits.
easy.explanation: Deadlines protect the caller's latency at the cost of ambiguity.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sets a 500 ms deadline on lookup(). Step 2: At 500 ms with no reply, it stops waiting and fails over. Step 3: The server may still finish later—the caller traded certainty for responsiveness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Deadlines bound waiting, not server execution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Storage quotas are unrelated to call latency bounds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Expiry leaves execution ambiguous.

easy.prompt: When is streaming RPC preferred over unary request-response?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When exactly one tiny value is exchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When the network forbids long connections.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When callers must never receive updates.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When delivering many messages over time—logs, market ticks, or large transfers—where per-call overhead would dominate.

easy.hint: Next step: count the handshakes for 10,000 unary calls vs one stream.
easy.explanation: One stream amortizes setup over many messages.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 10,000 price ticks as unary calls pay framing and header costs 10,000 times. Step 2: One stream pays setup once and frames each tick cheaply. Step 3: gRPC server-streaming over HTTP/2 multiplexes this efficiently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One small exchange is the unary sweet spot.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Streaming needs a sustained connection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Push updates are streaming's main use.

easy.prompt: What does linearizability guarantee for operations on a register?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its start and end, in one total order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reads may return values from five seconds ago forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Writes need manual administrator approval to appear.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Concurrent operations may be reordered against real time freely.

easy.hint: Next step: place each operation's 'instant' between its call and return.
easy.explanation: Linearizability ties the observed order to real time.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Write(x=1) finishes at t=5; read starting at t=6 must see 1. Step 2: Two overlapping writes may appear in either order, but once one finishes, later reads agree. Step 3: This is why linearizable stores coordinate on the write path.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a fixed staleness bound, not linearizability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Visibility is automatic, not operator-gated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real-time precedence across non-overlapping ops must be respected.

easy.prompt: A linearizable register completes write(x=7) at time 10. A read starting at time 11 returns 5. What happened?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reads never need to see completed writes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The system violated linearizability—unless a newer write of 5 completed between time 10 and the read.

choices.label: C
choices.body: This is always legal under linearizability.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Linearizability allows any stale value forever.

easy.hint: Next step: check real-time precedence between the write's end and the read's start.
easy.explanation: Completed writes must be visible to later-starting reads.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Write of 7 ends at t=10. Step 2: Read begins at t=11, after that completion. Step 3: Returning 5 means the read missed a write that preceded it in real time—a linearizability violation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Seeing completed writes is the core guarantee.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A stale read after a completed newer write breaks real-time order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Staleness must end once the newer write completes.

easy.prompt: Sequential consistency guarantees what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only UDP packets may carry writes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All operations appear in one total order that respects each process's program order, though real-time order across processes may differ.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Operations need no global order at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Real-time precedence across processes is always respected.

easy.hint: Next step: check each process's own operation order inside the global sequence.
easy.explanation: Per-process order is preserved; cross-process real-time order is not.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: P1 does a then b; P2 does c then d. Step 2: Global orders like a,c,b,d or c,a,d,b are legal if each process's pair stays ordered. Step 3: An order like b,...,a would violate P1's program order and is forbidden.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Transport protocol is unrelated to the memory model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sequential still provides a single global sequence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That extra clause is linearizability, not sequential.

easy.prompt: Eventual consistency guarantees what once updates stop?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The leader is permanently frozen.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All replicas converge to the same value.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every write is immediately rolled back.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Reads return random values forever.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what 'eventually' modifies: convergence, not immediacy.
easy.explanation: Without new writes, repair and propagation align all replicas.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Write v=9 reaches replicas A and B; C is partitioned. Step 2: Updates stop; the partition heals. Step 3: Anti-entropy copies v=9 to C—all three converge.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Leadership can change; convergence is about data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Eventual consistency keeps writes; it does not roll them back.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Convergence is the defining guarantee once writes halt.

easy.prompt: With N replicas, write quorum W, and read quorum R, which condition guarantees every read sees the latest completed write?

choices.label: A
choices.body: N = 1 always.

choices.label: B
choices.body: R + W > N, so every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica.

choices.label: D
choices.body: R = W = 1 regardless of N.

easy.hint: Next step: draw two subsets of replicas and force them to share a member.
easy.explanation: Overlap means the reader always meets a replica carrying the newest version.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: N=5, W=3, R=3: any 3-set shares ≥1 node with any other 3-set. Step 2: The writer puts v8 on its 3; the reader's 3 includes one of them. Step 3: Comparing versions, the reader picks v8—staleness impossible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A single replica removes all fault tolerance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero-sized quorums contact no replicas at all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Singleton quorums miss each other when N > 1.

easy.prompt: Why is 'a quorum always means a majority' wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: R+W>N can never hold without majorities.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Quorums forbid tuning read vs write cost.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Quorum only means overlapping sets with R+W>N; majorities are one convenient choice, but quorums can be asymmetric (e.g., W=4,R=2 with N=5).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Majorities never overlap with each other.

easy.hint: Next step: test R=2, W=4, N=5 against the overlap rule.
easy.explanation: Majority is sufficient for quorums, not necessary.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Writes touch 4 of 5 (expensive, durable); reads touch any 2 (cheap). Step 2: 4+2=6 > 5, so every read pair meets every write set. Step 3: Reads stay consistent while optimized for latency—no majority needed on the read path.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: W=4,R=2,N=5 satisfies 6>5 with R a minority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Asymmetry is exactly how systems bias toward cheap reads or writes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two majorities always overlap—that is why they work.

easy.prompt: What is a CRDT (conflict-free replicated data type)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A lock manager for two-phase locking.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An encryption scheme for stored data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A data type whose concurrent updates merge deterministically (commutative, associative, idempotent) so replicas converge without coordination.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A consensus protocol needing a leader.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what happens when two replicas merge in different orders.
easy.explanation: Order-independent merges make convergence automatic.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Replica A adds 'x', replica B adds 'y' concurrently. Step 2: A merges B's {y}, B merges A's {x}—both reach {x,y}. Step 3: Any merge order lands on the same set: that is the CRDT contract.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CRDTs are lock-free by construction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CRDTs are about merge semantics, not secrecy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CRDTs avoid leaders and coordination on the write path.

easy.prompt: How does gossip (epidemic) propagation spread an update?

choices.label: A
choices.body: By writing to every node in one atomic transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: By deleting the update from all peers at once.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers, so the update infects the cluster exponentially fast.

choices.label: D
choices.body: By broadcasting from a single leader in lockstep.

easy.hint: Next step: picture one infected node contacting two, then four.
easy.explanation: Random pairwise rounds give logarithmic-time coverage with no coordinator.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Node 1 tells nodes 4 and 9 about v3. Step 2: Those tell 2 others each next round. Step 3: Within ~log(N) rounds nearly all nodes carry v3—robust to individual failures.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Gossip is lazy and pairwise, not atomic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Gossip spreads data; it does not mass-delete.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Gossip is decentralized and randomized, not leader-driven.

easy.prompt: Read-your-writes consistency guarantees that a client sees what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only data from a different continent.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Nothing—reads always fail.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Its own prior writes on subsequent reads in the same session.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every other client's writes before they happen.

easy.hint: Next step: follow one client's session, not the whole world.
easy.explanation: A session sticks to replicas that have its updates, or waits until they arrive.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: You set avatar=v2 on replica A. Step 2: Your next read routed to stale replica B would show v1. Step 3: With read-your-writes, the router pins you to A (or version-gates B) so you see v2.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Geography is not the defining constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The guarantee is about visibility of own writes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That would be stronger than read-your-writes.

easy.prompt: In Paxos, what does a proposer send in the prepare phase, and what does it ask?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A ballot number n, asking acceptors to promise never to accept anything numbered below n.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A committed value with no ballot number.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A DNS lookup for the leader's address.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An order to delete all prior log entries.

easy.hint: Next step: name the number that outranks older proposals.
easy.explanation: Prepare(n) blocks lower ballots so at most one value can win per round.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Proposer P picks unused ballot 5 and broadcasts prepare(5). Step 2: Acceptors promising for 5 reject any accept numbered below 5. Step 3: Higher ballots supersede lower ones—dueling proposers resolve by ballot order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ballots order competing proposals; values come in the accept phase.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Naming is unrelated to Paxos phases.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Acceptors must retain state for safety.

easy.prompt: In Paxos, when is a value considered chosen?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When a majority of acceptors have accepted the same ballot and value.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When one proposer first suggests it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When one acceptor stores it locally.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When the client retries three times.

easy.hint: Next step: count acceptors, not messages sent.
easy.explanation: Majority acceptance is the commit point of a Paxos instance.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Proposer sends accept(6, X) to five acceptors. Step 2: Three reply accepted—majority reached, X is chosen even if the other two never answer. Step 3: Learners can now announce X; later ballots must re-propose X.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A suggestion is not agreement until a majority accepts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A single acceptor cannot speak for the cluster.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Retries are liveness traffic, not the choice rule.

easy.prompt: In Raft, when does a follower become a candidate?

choices.label: A
choices.body: After its election timeout elapses without hearing from the current leader.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediately when any client read arrives.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only when the cluster has zero nodes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Whenever the leader sends a heartbeat.

easy.hint: Next step: link missing heartbeats to leader suspicion.
easy.explanation: Expired heartbeats suggest a dead leader, starting a new election.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Leader sends heartbeats every 50 ms; follower timeout is 200 ms. Step 2: Leader crashes; 200 ms pass with silence. Step 3: The follower becomes candidate, increments its term, and requests votes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Client reads never start elections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Elections need live voters to grant votes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Heartbeats suppress elections; their absence triggers them.

easy.prompt: What must a Raft candidate obtain to become leader of its term?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Approval from the previous leader.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Votes from a majority of cluster nodes in that term.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Votes from every node unanimously.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A self-vote only, with no other support.

easy.hint: Next step: count votes against cluster size.
easy.explanation: Majority election guarantees at most one leader per term.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 5 nodes: candidate needs 3 votes including itself. Step 2: Two candidates splitting 2-2-1 means neither wins; timeouts retry. Step 3: At most one candidate can hold 3 votes per term—majorities intersect.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The old leader may be dead; votes come from peers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Unanimity would block progress during one failure; majority suffices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One vote is not a majority in a multi-node cluster.

easy.prompt: In Raft, how does the leader replicate a new client command?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It broadcasts the result without any log.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It appends the entry to its own log, sends AppendEntries to followers, and commits once a majority stores it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It asks followers to invent the entry independently.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It commits first and replicates later at leisure.

easy.hint: Next step: order the steps: append, send, commit, apply.
easy.explanation: Majority storage is the commit point; state machines apply after.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Leader appends op at index 8, term 3. Step 2: Three of five nodes store it—majority reached. Step 3: Leader marks index 8 committed, applies it, acks the client, and piggybacks the commit index to followers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Durability needs the replicated log.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Only the leader orders entries; followers copy them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Commit requires majority replication before acking.

easy.prompt: What role do monotonically increasing terms (Raft) or ballot numbers (Paxos) play?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They compress old log segments automatically.

choices.label: B
choices.body: They assign clients to shards by hash.

choices.label: C
choices.body: They order leadership eras so stale leaders and old proposals are recognized and rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.body: They encrypt log entries against followers.

easy.hint: Next step: ask how a node spots an outdated leader.
easy.explanation: Higher term wins; lower-term messages are stale by definition.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Leader of term 3 partitions away; followers elect term 4. Step 2: Old leader returns sending term-3 heartbeats. Step 3: Followers reject them (3 < 4) and the old leader steps down—no split-brain writes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Snapshotting compacts logs; terms order authority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Shard placement is partitioning, not consensus terms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Terms are plain metadata, not encryption.

easy.prompt: Why do Raft and Paxos require majorities for elections and commits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Majority means literally all nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Minorities cannot store any data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Any two majorities overlap, so at most one leader per term and at most one value per instance can win.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Majorities make every operation faster.

easy.hint: Next step: draw two 3-of-5 sets and find their shared member.
easy.explanation: Overlap is the whole safety argument.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 5 nodes: leader needs 3 votes; commit needs 3 stores. Step 2: Any two 3-sets share ≥1 node. Step 3: That shared node blocks a second leader or a conflicting commit—split-brain decisions are impossible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Majority is floor(n/2)+1, not unanimity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Minorities store data; they just cannot decide alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Majorities cost round trips; they buy safety, not speed.

easy.prompt: A 5-node cluster splits 3 versus 2. Which side can elect a Raft leader, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both sides can elect leaders simultaneously.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the 2-node side, since minorities are faster.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Neither side until the partition heals.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the 3-node side: it alone can assemble a majority of 3.

easy.hint: Next step: count votes available on each side.
easy.explanation: Majority-side availability with minority-side blocking is the CAP tradeoff in action.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Side A has 3 votes available—enough to elect and commit. Step 2: Side B has at most 2—every candidacy stalls. Step 3: Clients on side B must wait or fail over; their writes cannot diverge.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The 2-node side can never reach 3 votes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed does not grant votes; counts do.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The majority side proceeds normally during partitions.

easy.prompt: In Raft, what is the difference between a committed entry and an applied entry?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Applied entries may be lost freely.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Commit happens after the client times out.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Committed means stored on a majority (durable); applied means the state machine has executed it locally.

choices.label: D
choices.body: They are identical with no distinction.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what survives a leader crash.
easy.explanation: Majority storage protects committed entries; each node applies them at its own pace.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Entry stored on 3/5: committed, client acked. Step 2: Leader applied it; a follower lags, not yet applied. Step 3: If the leader crashes, the entry persists on the majority and the new leader drives everyone to apply it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Committed entries are never lost; application follows commitment.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Commit precedes the client ack.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Commit is cluster-wide durability; apply is local execution.

easy.prompt: What are the two phases of two-phase commit (2PC)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Prepare (vote): participants promise to commit; then commit/abort: the coordinator broadcasts the final decision.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compile and link.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encrypt and decrypt.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Boot and shutdown.

easy.hint: Next step: separate voting from deciding.
easy.explanation: Participants vote in phase one; the coordinator decides in phase two.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Coordinator sends prepare; each participant votes YES (durable, locked) or NO. Step 2: If all YES, coordinator sends COMMIT; otherwise ABORT. Step 3: Participants obey the decision—unanimous YES is required to commit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Those are build steps, not transaction phases.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 2PC is about agreement, not cryptography.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Machine power states are unrelated to 2PC.

easy.prompt: In 2PC, what does a participant's YES vote promise?

choices.label: A
choices.body: That it crashed and will never answer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: That it is prepared: it holds locks, logged the update durably, and will commit if told to.

choices.label: C
choices.body: That it already committed unilaterally.

choices.label: D
choices.body: That it deleted its copy of the data.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what the participant must be able to do after voting YES.
easy.explanation: YES surrenders the right to decide unilaterally until the coordinator resolves.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Participant logs the write and locks the rows, replying YES. Step 2: It now waits—neither committing nor aborting on its own. Step 3: On COMMIT it applies; on ABORT it rolls back and releases locks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: YES means alive, ready, and waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Commit waits for the coordinator's phase-two decision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: It preserves the update pending the decision.

easy.prompt: The saga pattern handles multi-service transactions by doing what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Storing all state only in browser cookies.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Chaining local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it on failure.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Running one giant 2PC across 500 microservices.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Forbidding any rollback or undo.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what undoes step 1 after step 3 fails.
easy.explanation: Each step commits locally; compensations run in reverse on failure.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Book flight (committed), book hotel (committed), charge card (fails). Step 2: Saga runs cancel-hotel then cancel-flight. Step 3: No global locks were ever held—consistency is semantic and eventual.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Durable saga state lives in services and databases.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sagas avoid long-lived global 2PC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Compensating transactions are explicit semantic rollbacks.

easy.prompt: In the CAP theorem, what do C, A, and P stand for?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Compression, Archiving, and Parallelism.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Concurrency, Authentication, and Privacy.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Caching, Allocation, and Persistence.

easy.hint: Next step: expand each letter as a system property.
easy.explanation: CAP names the three properties traded off when networks partition.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Consistency here means linearizability: all nodes agree. Step 2: Availability means every request gets a (non-error) response. Step 3: Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite message loss between groups.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CAP does not refer to storage compression or archiving.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Those are security and programming concerns, not CAP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CAP is about consistency, availability, and partitions.

easy.prompt: PACELC extends CAP by stating that else (E), even without partitions, one often trades between what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: CPU brand and keyboard layout.

choices.label: B
choices.body: File extension and MIME type.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Latency and consistency.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Password length and certificate color.

easy.hint: Next step: read the E clause: 'else, latency vs consistency'.
easy.explanation: When the network is healthy, coordination choices still cost latency.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Sync quorum write: consistent, waits for replicas. Step 2: Single-replica write: fast, briefly divergent. Step 3: Same healthy network, different latency-consistency point per operation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hardware peripherals are unrelated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Web typing is unrelated to database tradeoffs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PACELC concerns latency and consistency, not credentials.

easy.prompt: What is hash partitioning of a key space?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sorting keys alphabetically on one machine.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encrypting keys with a public certificate.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Assigning each key to a shard via a hash function over the key.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Storing every key on every node for every query.

easy.hint: Next step: follow one key from hash value to shard owner.
easy.explanation: Hashing spreads keys evenly for scalable storage.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Key 'user:42' hashes to 0x9F3A. Step 2: 0x9F3A mod 8 shards = shard 2. Step 3: All operations on that key route to shard 2's replicas.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That does not distribute across nodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Partitioning is about placement, not encryption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is full replication, not partitioning.

easy.prompt: A hot partition (hot spot) occurs when what happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: All shards sit idle with zero traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every key hashes to its own datacenter.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The network has zero latency everywhere.

choices.label: D
choices.body: One shard receives disproportionately many accesses for its key range.

easy.hint: Next step: look for skewed access, not skewed data size.
easy.explanation: Celebrity keys or time-ordered IDs hammer one shard.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Range sharding by timestamp sends all of today's writes to the tail shard. Step 2: That shard saturates while others idle. Step 3: Fixes: hash the key, split the range, or add caching in front.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hot spots imply concentrated high load.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would be over-sharding, not a hot-spot definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Latency does not define partition skew.

easy.prompt: What does Jepsen-style testing do to a distributed database?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Benchmarks single-node sorting speed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Audits password strength policies.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Measures CSS rendering performance.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Injects faults (partitions, clock skew, kills) during a workload and checks whether observed histories violate claimed guarantees.

easy.hint: Next step: think 'faults in, history out, checker judges'.
easy.explanation: Nemesis plus workload plus consistency checker is the Jepsen loop.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Workload writes and reads while the nemesis partitions the cluster. Step 2: Every operation is logged with timing. Step 3: The checker (e.g., Elle) searches for cycles proving lost updates or stale reads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Jepsen tests distributed correctness under faults, not sort speed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Credential audits are unrelated to consistency testing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Frontend rendering is out of scope.

easy.prompt: Strict two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees serializability by which rule?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Releasing each lock immediately after use.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Never acquiring any locks at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Holding locks forever after commit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Transactions acquire locks as needed but release none until commit/abort (growing then shrinking phase).

easy.hint: Next step: split the transaction into a growing phase and a shrinking phase.
easy.explanation: Holding all locks to commit orders conflicting transactions serially.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: T1 locks A, then B (growing). Step 2: T1 commits and releases both (shrinking). Step 3: Any T2 touching A or B either waits fully before or after T1—equivalent to a serial order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Early release lets others see uncommitted state—breaks isolation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Lock-free needs OCC or MVCC machinery instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Locks release at commit; holding longer only blocks throughput.

medium.prompt: Partial synchrony (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer) assumes what about timing bounds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No bounds ever hold and stabilization never comes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every node carries an atomic GPS clock.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Finite bounds exist but are unknown, or they hold only after some unknown stabilization time (GST).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bounds are known from the very start of execution.

medium.hint: Next step: contrast 'bounds exist but are unknown' with 'bounds are known'.
medium.explanation: Partial synchrony sits between sync and async: bounds are real but you cannot name them in advance.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Before GST the network behaves asynchronously, so safety must never depend on timing. Step 2: After GST, unknown bounds hold, so liveness tools like Raft timeouts eventually work. Step 3: Protocols therefore guarantee safety always and progress only after stabilization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is pure asynchrony; partial synchrony adds eventual bounds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Physical clocks are a mechanism, not the partial-synchrony definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Known-from-start bounds are full synchrony, not partial synchrony.

medium.prompt: How does the crash-recovery model differ from crash-stop?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Recovery is always instant and lossless.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A crashed node may restart later, so it must recover state from stable storage and rejoin carefully.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A restarted node may lie arbitrarily to peers.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Restarted nodes need no persisted state at all.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what survives the crash.
medium.explanation: Recovery adds stable storage plus a rejoin protocol; a restarted node must not replay stale writes as new.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Node writes W to disk, crashes before acknowledging. Step 2: On restart it replays its log—without a persisted record it could lose or duplicate W. Step 3: Hence crash-recovery systems persist intent first, then rejoin with epoch fencing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Restart takes time and unflushed state can be lost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Arbitrary lies are Byzantine faults, not crash-recovery.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Without stable storage a restarted node cannot resume its log position.

medium.prompt: In a synchronous replication setting, how many replicas are needed to tolerate f crash-stop failures while keeping one working copy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only f-1 replicas when f > 0.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always 3f+1 replicas.

choices.label: C
choices.body: At least f+1 replicas, so one survives any f crashes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exactly one replica in total.

medium.hint: Next step: count the survivors when the worst case hits.
medium.explanation: f crashes leave (f+1) - f = 1 live copy holding the data.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: With 3 replicas and f=2, two crashes still leave one copy. Step 2: With only 2 replicas and f=2, both may die and data is lost. Step 3: Note voting schemes often use 2f+1 for majority overlap—stronger than this availability minimum.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Fewer than f+1 replicas can all die under f failures.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 3f+1 is the Byzantine quorum size, not the crash-stop availability minimum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One replica cannot survive even a single failure.

medium.prompt: A client resends a request three times; the server log shows it never arrived, yet the server handles other clients normally. Replies toward this client also vanish. Which diagnosis fits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wall-clock skew dropped the packets.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Omission faults on this client's paths—receive-omission at the server or send-omission on the return path.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The server suffered a crash-stop failure.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The server is Byzantine and equivocating.

medium.hint: Next step: eliminate every model contradicted by 'serves others normally'.
medium.explanation: A live server missing one client's traffic points to lossy links or buffers—in other words, omission.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Crash-stop is ruled out because the server answers everyone else. Step 2: Byzantine needs conflicting content; none is observed. Step 3: The remaining explanation is selective loss—check buffers and firewall rules, and fix with retries plus dedup.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Clock skew affects ordering, not packet delivery.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A halted server could not keep serving the other clients.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No conflicting or malicious content was observed, only loss.

medium.prompt: PBFT-style Byzantine agreement with 3f+1 total replicas tolerates how many Byzantine faults?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Up to f Byzantine replicas.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Up to 2f+1 Byzantine replicas.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Zero—it handles crash-stop faults only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All replicas except one, regardless of f.

medium.hint: Next step: recall why quorums of 2f+1 must intersect in a correct node.
medium.explanation: Quorums of size 2f+1 overlap in at least f+1 nodes, so one correct node witnesses every pair of decisions.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: With 4 nodes (f=1), quorums of 3 intersect in 2 nodes—at least one is honest. Step 2: Two conflicting decisions would each need honest witnesses, impossible with a single liar. Step 3: Hence at most f liars can be outvoted safely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would exceed the designed fault threshold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: PBFT explicitly targets Byzantine faults.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tolerance is bounded by f, not by an arbitrary faulty majority.

medium.prompt: Why is Byzantine tolerance fundamentally harder than crash tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Byzantine faults affect only disks, never messages.

choices.label: B
choices.body: You cannot trust any single message; evidence must come from quorums and authentication, not one sender.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Byzantine nodes never send anything at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Crash faults already include lying.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what one received message proves.
medium.explanation: One message proves nothing when the sender may lie, so protocols cross-check across replicas.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: A crashed node's silence is self-evident; a liar's message looks valid. Step 2: Replicas therefore exchange signed prepare and commit certificates before deciding. Step 3: The extra phases and 3f+1 sizing are the price of distrust.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Equivocation over messages is the defining danger.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Total silence is crash-stop behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Crash-stop excludes equivocation by definition.

medium.prompt: What indistinguishability argument drives the FLP result?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A slow process and a crashed process look identical to others for any finite waiting period.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Crashed nodes always send explicit error codes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Wall clocks reliably expose crashed nodes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: TCP reliably reports remote crashes to the app.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what any finite wait proves.
medium.explanation: No finite timeout separates 'dead' from 'very slow' under asynchrony.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Node P waits 5 s for Q's message; nothing arrives. Step 2: Q may have crashed at t=0, or its message may arrive at t=6. Step 3: Any decision P makes now is wrong in one of the two indistinguishable executions—so deterministic termination fails.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A halted node sends nothing, exactly like a very slow one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clocks measure local time, not remote liveness, under asynchrony.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TCP retransmits and stalls; it cannot prove a peer is dead.

medium.prompt: Which design choice lets practical systems like Raft sidestep FLP?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Elect leaders without requiring majorities.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Assume partial synchrony: use timeouts and heartbeats so liveness holds once the network stabilizes, while safety never depends on timing.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Assume processes never fail.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Run consensus over UDP without retries.

medium.hint: Next step: separate safety-always from liveness-eventually.
medium.explanation: Raft is safe during async execution and live once timeouts become meaningful after GST.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Raft's voting rules (majority, monotonic terms) guarantee at most one leader per term with no timing assumption. Step 2: Election timeouts only drive progress; wrong suspicions cause extra terms, not wrong commits. Step 3: After GST some candidate completes an election and the log advances—FLP is dodged, not refuted.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: elections without majorities risk split-brain instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Raft explicitly tolerates crash failures with majorities.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unreliable delivery alone does not escape FLP.

medium.prompt: What is the tradeoff when tuning a failure-detector timeout?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Short timeouts detect real crashes fast but raise false suspicions; long timeouts are accurate but slow to react.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Short timeouts are better in every way.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Long timeouts are better in every way.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The timeout value controls disk capacity.

medium.hint: Next step: plot false positives against detection speed.
medium.explanation: Timeout tuning trades speed for accuracy.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: A 50 ms timeout starts failover in 50 ms but fires on every GC pause. Step 2: A 5 s timeout never false-fires yet leaves the service degraded for 5 s per real crash. Step 3: Production systems adapt timeouts (phi-accrual detectors) instead of fixing one value.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Aggressive timeouts fire on every GC pause.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Conservative timeouts leave outages undetected for seconds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Timeouts govern detection speed and accuracy, not storage.

medium.prompt: Monitor M misses heartbeats from S for 3 intervals, marks S 'suspected', then receives a delayed heartbeat with a higher sequence number. What should M do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ignore all future heartbeats from S.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Clear the suspicion and treat S as alive; the newer sequence number is fresh evidence of life.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Keep S marked dead forever.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Declare S Byzantine for sending late data.

medium.hint: Next step: check what a newer sequence number proves.
medium.explanation: Suspicions are revocable; fresh evidence overrides them.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: The suspicion rested on absence of news, which delay fully explains. Step 2: A heartbeat with a newer sequence number is positive evidence of liveness after the suspicion. Step 3: M revokes suspicion—this unreliable-detector pattern is what Raft-style liveness relies on.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Fresh heartbeats are exactly the signal a detector needs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Suspicions are revocable when contrary evidence arrives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lateness alone is not equivocation or malice.

medium.prompt: What is the Lamport clock update rule on send and receive?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Increment before each local event and send; on receive, set the clock to max(local, received) + 1.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Set the clock exactly to the received stamp.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reset the clock to zero on every receive.

choices.label: A
choices.body: To let the proposer delete old values.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To elect a new leader immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.body: So the new proposer re-proposes that value instead of a conflicting one, preserving a choice that may already have been made.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To waste bandwidth with extra gossip.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what happens if a quorum already chose value X.
medium.explanation: Re-proposing X keeps every later ballot consistent with the earlier choice.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: A quorum accepted (4, X); the choice of X is decided but P never heard. Step 2: P's prepare(6) reaches a majority, one member reporting (4, X). Step 3: P must propose X at ballot 6—any quorum for 6 overlaps the deciding one, so X propagates instead of conflicting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Old values must be honored, not deleted.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Leader election is Raft's framing; Paxos uses ballots per instance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The report is the core safety mechanism, not overhead.

medium.prompt: An acceptor promised ballot 8 but now receives accept(6, X). What must it do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Crash itself to avoid deciding.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reject it: the acceptor already promised never to accept anything below ballot 8.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Accept it, since X may be important.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Accept it and lower its promise to 6.

medium.hint: Next step: compare the accept's number with the recorded promise.
medium.explanation: The promise is a firewall against superseded ballots.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Promised=8 after prepare(8). Step 2: accept(6,X) arrives numbered below the promise. Step 3: Rejection forces the stale proposer to retry with a higher ballot, where it will learn any chosen value.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Crashing changes liveness, not the promise rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Honoring stale ballots would fork the decision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Promises only move upward, never downward.

medium.prompt: A Paxos learner hears that a majority accepted (6, X) but some acceptors report never accepting anything. What should the learner conclude?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The value must be re-proposed at ballot 1.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two values are now chosen simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.body: X is chosen: majority acceptance decides the instance regardless of silent minorities.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing is chosen until every acceptor accepts.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what a majority implies about every other majority.
medium.explanation: Any two majorities intersect, so no conflicting value can also reach majority.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Majority M1 accepted (6,X). Step 2: Any rival value Y needs its own majority M2. Step 3: M1 and M2 share an acceptor that accepted X at 6 and promised accordingly—Y cannot complete there.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Restarting at low ballots reopens contention pointlessly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Majority overlap forbids a second chosen value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unanimity is not required; majorities decide.

medium.prompt: Why does Raft randomize election timeouts across followers?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To make every election take exactly the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To let leaders serve stale reads safely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: To make simultaneous candidacies unlikely, so one candidate wins quickly instead of repeated split votes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To guarantee the most-up-to-date log always wins.

medium.hint: Next step: picture all followers timing out in the same millisecond.
medium.explanation: Staggered timeouts elect a first candidate before rivals wake.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Three followers share a 200 ms timeout; leader dies; all three become candidates and split votes. Step 2: Nobody reaches majority; new timeouts fire together again. Step 3: With 150–300 ms randomized timeouts, one candidate starts first, gathers votes, and wins before others compete.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Jitter deliberately varies timeouts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Read safety comes from leases/read-index, not timeout jitter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Log checks restrict voting, but timing splits still need jitter.

medium.prompt: A Raft candidate receives a heartbeat carrying a higher term. What must it do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ignore the heartbeat and keep campaigning.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Decrement its own term and retry.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete its log and restart the cluster.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Step down to follower, update its term, and accept the newer leader's authority.

medium.hint: Next step: compare the two terms.
medium.explanation: The higher term proves a newer authority exists.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Candidate at term 4 gets AppendEntries with term 5. Step 2: Term 5 > 4 means a newer election already resolved elsewhere. Step 3: The candidate reverts to follower at term 5, preserving single-leader-per-term safety.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Higher terms always supersede; ignoring them forks leadership.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Terms never decrease.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Logs persist; only the role and term change.

medium.prompt: Raft's log-matching property says: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the last entries must match.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Terms must decrease after the match.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The logs are identical in all preceding entries.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The logs may differ arbitrarily before that index.

medium.hint: Next step: induct backward from the matching entry.
medium.explanation: The leader's consistency check enforces prefix agreement.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Leader sends AppendEntries with prevIndex=7, prevTerm=3. Step 2: A follower lacking (7,3) rejects, and the leader backs up until prefixes align. Step 3: Hence any two logs agreeing at (index, term) share every earlier entry.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Safety depends on the whole prefix agreeing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Terms are non-decreasing along a log.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Matching index-plus-term implies identical prefixes.

medium.prompt: A Raft leader commits entry (term=2, index=5) on a majority, then crashes before followers apply it. Can the new leader drop this entry?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes, unapplied entries may always be discarded.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Yes, if the new term is higher.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes, a majority of the new term can overwrite it.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No—leader completeness forces the new leader's log to contain every committed entry.

medium.hint: Next step: ask who could have won the election without that entry.
medium.explanation: Election majorities overlap commit majorities, so the winner holds the entry.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Entry committed on {A,B,C}; C crashes as leader. Step 2: Any new majority (3 of 5) includes at least one of A/B/C. Step 3: Voters' log-freshness check steers leadership to a node carrying index 5—committed data survives.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Commitment, not application, is what durability protects.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Higher terms never erase committed entries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Majorities extend committed prefixes; they do not rewrite them.

medium.prompt: A partitioned old leader keeps receiving client writes it cannot replicate. What should it do once it learns of a higher term?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Keep acking writes from its stale log.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Increment its term past the new leader unilaterally.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete the higher-term messages as spam.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Step down immediately and stop serving writes; its authority expired with the term.

medium.hint: Next step: check whether it can still reach a majority.
medium.explanation: Minority leaders must go silent to protect the commit history.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Old leader at term 3 holds 1 of 5 nodes; term 4 leads the other 4. Step 2: Any write it acks exists only on its minority—uncommitted and invisible. Step 3: On seeing term 4 it becomes follower; clients retry on the majority side.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Acking without majority replication forks committed history.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Terms advance via elections, not self-promotion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Higher terms are authoritative and must be honored.

medium.prompt: How many failures can a 2f+1-node Raft cluster tolerate while still electing leaders and committing?

choices.label: A
choices.body: f failures: a majority of f+1 nodes remains reachable.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 2f+1 failures.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Zero failures ever.

choices.label: D
choices.body: f-1 failures only.

medium.hint: Next step: subtract failures from 2f+1 and check for a majority.
medium.explanation: (2f+1) − f = f+1, exactly a majority.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 5 nodes (f=2): lose any 2, 3 remain—a majority. Step 2: Lose 3, only 2 remain—elections stall, commits block. Step 3: The cluster trades availability under big partitions for never committing conflicting histories.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No nodes would remain to vote.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Single-failure tolerance is the point of 3-node clusters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That undersells the majority math by one.

medium.prompt: Why does a Raft leader only consider entries from its own term committed by counting replicas, while older-term entries commit indirectly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Old-term entries can never commit at all.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Counting replicas is unnecessary for new entries.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Terms have no effect on commitment.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A new leader may hold uncommitted old-term entries; committing one new entry anchors the whole prefix including them.

medium.hint: Next step: picture a deposed leader's uncommitted entry lingering on a majority.
medium.explanation: Blindly counting old-term replicas could commit something the new leader is allowed to overwrite.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: L1 (term 2) spreads E to 3/5 but never commits it; L2 (term 3) wins without E... wait, leader completeness would force E along—precisely the subtle case. Step 2: Raft refuses to commit E by counting alone; it commits a term-3 no-op/entry first. Step 3: That commit point covers the prefix, safely finalizing E only as part of term 3's history.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They commit once a newer entry from the current term covers them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Majority counting is exactly the commit rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The term restriction closes a known safety hole with deposed leaders.

medium.prompt: A follower applies log entries as soon as they arrive, before learning they are committed. What anomaly can clients see after a leader change?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Dirty reads of uncommitted data that is later overwritten—clients saw effects that never became durable history.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No anomaly; early apply is always safe.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The follower's disk fills instantly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The leader loses its own committed prefix.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what happens to that entry if the leader deposes.
medium.explanation: State machines must trail commitment, never lead it.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Follower applies uncommitted E and serves a read showing it. Step 2: New leader overwrites E with E' (legal: E was uncommitted). Step 3: The client saw E, but history now says E'—apply only up to the known commit index.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Uncommitted entries may vanish under a new leader.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Storage is not the issue; visibility of rolled-back state is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The leader's log is authoritative; the follower showed speculative state.

medium.prompt: If the 2PC coordinator crashes after all participants voted YES but before sending COMMIT, what happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: All data is instantly deleted on every node.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Partitions become permanently impossible.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Participants block holding locks until the coordinator recovers—2PC's blocking problem.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Participants automatically commit without recovery.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what an in-doubt participant safely may do.
medium.explanation: Uncertain outcome plus held locks equals unavailability.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Three participants voted YES and wait for the decision. Step 2: The coordinator is down, so no COMMIT or ABORT arrives. Step 3: Locks pile up and conflicting transactions queue—throughput on those rows drops to zero until recovery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blocking holds locks; it does not wipe data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Partitions remain possible; 2PC is fragile under failures.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: In-doubt participants must wait; unilateral commit risks divergence.

medium.prompt: Why is '2PC is fault-tolerant' a misconception?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 2PC handles coordinator crashes with zero blocking.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 2PC never holds locks across failures.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 2PC is equivalent to Paxos-backed commit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 2PC tolerates single participant failures poorly: coordinator loss blocks everyone, and recovery needs the coordinator's log.

medium.hint: Next step: crash each role on paper and watch who waits.
medium.explanation: 2PC is an agreement protocol that itself needs a fault-tolerant decision record.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Crash a participant before voting: coordinator aborts—fine. Step 2: Crash the coordinator after YES votes: everyone blocks—bad. Step 3: Production systems replicate the coordinator state (or use 3PC/Paxos-commit) to escape the block.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Coordinator failure is exactly the blocking case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: In-doubt participants hold locks while waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Plain 2PC lacks a replicated decision log; hardened variants add consensus.

medium.prompt: When is a saga preferable to 2PC for a checkout flow across order, payment, and shipping services?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When all steps share one database and one lock manager.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When compensations are impossible to define.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When the steps are long-lived and owned by different teams—holding distributed locks for minutes is infeasible.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When strict atomicity with zero visible intermediate state is required.

medium.hint: Next step: compare lock-holding time in each design.
medium.explanation: Sagas trade isolation for availability and autonomy.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 2PC would lock order, payment, and shipping rows for the whole user checkout. Step 2: A slow fraud check stalls every service's rows. Step 3: Saga commits each step in milliseconds and compensates on failure—no cross-service lock waits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A single DB can use a local transaction instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Without compensations there is no saga.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sagas expose intermediate commits; strict atomicity needs 2PC or workflows with isolation.

medium.prompt: A saga books a flight, then fails to book the hotel, then its cancel-flight compensation also fails. What must the saga infrastructure do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Give up and declare the trip half-booked forever.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Roll back using a database ROLLBACK.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete the saga log to hide the failure.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Retry the compensation durably (with backoff and alerting) until it succeeds—compensations must be retryable and idempotent.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what record keeps the compensation alive across crashes.
medium.explanation: Durable saga logs plus idempotent compensations guarantee eventual cleanup.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Hotel failure triggers cancel-flight(id=7). Step 2: Airline API times out; saga log retains the pending compensation. Step 3: Retries with the same idempotency key eventually cancel—at-least-once compensation converges.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Abandoning leaves money and inventory inconsistent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The flight booking already committed externally; only semantic compensation works.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The log is what drives compensation retries to completion.

medium.prompt: During a network partition, why can a system not offer both strong consistency and full availability?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TLS handshakes fail on every link.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disk quotas are exceeded on all replicas.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Answering every request on isolated sides without coordination risks divergent state, so one property must yield.

choices.label: D
choices.body: CPUs become too slow to process packets.

medium.hint: Next step: put one writer on each side of the split.
medium.explanation: Isolated writers without communication cannot stay consistent and available at once.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Partition splits 5 nodes into 2 and 3. Step 2: Both sides accept writes to stay available: histories fork. Step 3: Reads now disagree—consistency lost. Refusing one side preserves consistency but sacrifices availability.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Security handshakes are unrelated to the CAP tradeoff.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Storage limits do not define CAP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CAP is a logical tradeoff, not a CPU speed limit.

medium.prompt: A CP system under partition typically does what to preserve consistency?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Serves every request on all sides with the latest data.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deletes all data on the majority partition.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disables authentication on all nodes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Rejects or blocks operations on the minority or unreachable side until the partition heals.

medium.hint: Next step: ask which side can still reach a quorum.
medium.explanation: Sacrificing minority availability avoids inconsistent reads and writes.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 5 nodes split 3/2; the 2-node side cannot form majorities. Step 2: Its writes block or return errors instead of forking history. Step 3: On healing, the minority replays the majority log and resumes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That risks split-brain divergence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CP systems block or redirect; they do not wipe majority data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Security policy is unrelated to CP behavior.

medium.prompt: A product team wants globally consistent leaderboards with 50 ms p99 writes across continents. What does PACELC say?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Add more threads to beat the speed of light.

choices.label: B
choices.body: CAP forbids any leaderboard at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Compress the payload to skip coordination.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Physics plus coordination forbid it: intercontinental round trips exceed 50 ms, so pick lower latency (eventual) or higher latency (consistent).

medium.explanation: ~150-200 ms RTT makes 50 ms strong writes physically impossible.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Leader in us-east, voter in eu-west: each quorum round ~90 ms+. Step 2: Commit needs at least one such round—budget blown. Step 3: Either serve regional leaderboards (eventual global merge) or raise the latency budget.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Concurrency does not shorten round-trip latency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Leaderboards exist; the tradeoff is freshness vs speed.
