medium.prompt: How should an API expose the PACELC tradeoff to different use cases?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Offer per-request consistency levels (e.g., ONE vs QUORUM vs ALL) so reads/writes pick their latency point.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hardcode one level for all operations forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Expose raw disk sectors to clients.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Remove all quorum options to simplify docs.

medium.hint: Next step: match each operation to its staleness budget.
medium.explanation: 'Like' counts read at ONE; balance transfers write at QUORUM.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Feed render at R=1: fast, maybe seconds stale—fine. Step 2: Payment commit at W=QUORUM: slower, durable and visible—required. Step 3: One cluster serves both by varying R/W per request.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One size fits neither likes-counters nor payments.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clients need consistency knobs, not hardware.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Removing choice forces every workload onto one bad point.

medium.prompt: Range partitioning can cause hot spots when keys are what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sequential or highly correlated, e.g., time-ordered IDs landing in one range.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Uniformly random across the key space.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hashed with a good function into many shards.

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Adjacent keys share a shard, concentrating load.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: IDs 1M–2M all live on shard S. Step 2: Tonight's signups write IDs 1.9M+—all to S. Step 3: S melts while other shards idle; hash or compound keys (user_id + timestamp) to scatter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random keys spread load—they prevent hot spots.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No writes imply no access hot spot.

medium.prompt: Consistent hashing reduces data movement when what changes?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: The client switches from HTTP to gRPC.

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Only keys near the changed ring segments remap, not the whole space.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 4 nodes own ring quarters; a 5th joins and takes slices from neighbors. Step 2: Only ~1/5 of keys move, versus ~all with mod-N hashing. Step 3: Virtual nodes smooth the slices so load stays even.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Cipher upgrades do not re-home keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Protocol choice does not remap keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Credential rotation is unrelated to placement.

medium.prompt: A Jepsen run reports a 'lost update' anomaly. What does that mean concretely?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: A write was correctly rejected by validation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reads were slightly slower than usual.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Two clients wrote different keys.

medium.explanation: Durability plus visibility failed for a confirmed write.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Client A appends x=1, gets success. Step 2: Partition heals; client B reads and never sees x=1. Step 3: The checker flags it: the system confirmed what it later forgot.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rejections are not acknowledged successes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Latency is not a correctness anomaly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Different keys cannot conflict; lost update hits the same key.

medium.prompt: Two transactions lock rows in opposite order (T1: A then B; T2: B then A). What classic hazard arises, and how is it handled?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Livelock from CPU spin only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Split-brain from network partition.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Byzantine equivocation between rows.

medium.explanation: Opposite orders create cycles; prevention (ordered locking) or detection (victim abort) resolves them.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: T1 holds A waits B; T2 holds B waits A—cycle. Step 2: Detector finds the cycle (or timeout fires). Step 3: T2 aborts, releases B; T1 proceeds, then T2 retries.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is lock-waiting deadlock, not scheduler livelock.

hard.prompt: An engineer ports a synchronous leader-election algorithm with a 200 ms timeout onto an asynchronous datacenter network. During congestion plus a GC pause, a live leader's heartbeat arrives at 350 ms. What happens?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Network partitions become impossible afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Linearizability is preserved automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Followers wrongly suspect the live leader and may start a spurious election.

hard.explanation: In async networks lateness carries no information, so the timeout fires on a healthy leader.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: leader alive, heartbeat delayed 350 ms past the 200 ms timeout. Step 2: Followers time out, declare the leader dead, increment terms, and vote. Step 3: The old leader returns, causing dueling elections and churn—correctness needs async-safe design, not fixed timeouts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: In async networks lateness carries no information, so expiry proves nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Timing assumptions do not prevent partitions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Spurious elections churn terms; consistency needs quorum rules, not timeouts.

hard.prompt: Node X stays alive but its NIC drops 30% of outbound packets; node Y halts entirely. Which failure classes fit?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both are crash-stop failures.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both are Byzantine failures.

choices.label: C
choices.body: X is Byzantine and Y shows omission.

choices.label: D
choices.body: X shows omission failures, Y a crash-stop failure.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether each faulty node keeps executing.
hard.explanation: Omission means alive but lossy; crash-stop means halted.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: X's process still runs and some messages arrive intact, so it is not halted. Step 2: Y sends nothing ever again and never lies, so it is not equivocating. Step 3: Treating X as merely crashed would miss its intermittent behavior—retransmission, not just failover, is needed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: X keeps executing, so it has not halted.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neither node equivocates or sends malicious content.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: X only drops packets (omission); Y halted fully (crash-stop).

hard.prompt: Why do omission failures complicate quorum protocols more than pure crash-stop failures?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Crash-stop failures are strictly harder to handle.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Omissions make the network synchronous.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A lossy-but-alive node may answer some quorums and miss others, creating inconsistent views that mimic disagreement.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Omission nodes always send malicious lies.

hard.hint: Next step: picture a node that votes 'yes' on one side of a partition only.
hard.explanation: Partial participation skews quorum reasoning that assumes members are either fully in or fully out.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: N=3, W=2; node C applies write w but its ack is dropped. Step 2: The writer completes on {A,B} while a later reader contacting {B,C} can see a stale mix. Step 3: Protocols add read-repair and version comparison to heal what crash-stop-only reasoning would miss.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A halted node is simply absent, which quorum math handles cleanly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Loss says nothing about timing bounds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Omission drops messages; it does not fabricate them.

hard.prompt: In a 4-node PBFT group (f=1), the leader sends PRE-PREPARE(seq=5, value=X) to two backups and PRE-PREPARE(seq=5, value=Y) to the third. A backup compares notes with peers. What should it conclude?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pick whichever value hashes higher and commit it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The leader equivocated—Byzantine behavior—so backups must trigger a view change rather than commit either value.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Treat this as a crash-stop and keep waiting.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether one leader may assign two values to a single sequence number.
hard.explanation: The same sequence number carrying two values is proof of leader misbehavior.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: seq 5 maps to X on some replicas and Y on another—no single order exists. Step 2: Honest backups collect both signed messages as evidence of equivocation. Step 3: They abandon this view, elect a new leader, and carry certificates forward so seq 5 is decided exactly once.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Committing without certificates risks finalizing the liar's fork.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hash comparison is not agreement; certificates and a new view are required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A halted leader sends nothing; this leader sent conflicting orders.

hard.prompt: Three nodes run a deterministic async voting protocol. A and B voted 0 and 1; C's message is delayed indefinitely by the scheduler. What does FLP say about this execution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: C's crash is detectable, so A and B should decide now.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deterministic protocols always terminate in this state.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The scheduler can keep the system undecided forever by withholding C's deciding message whenever a decision is imminent.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A and B must decide within one round regardless.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which single delayed message keeps both outcomes reachable.
hard.explanation: An adversarial schedule preserves bivalence by withholding the pivotal message.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: With C hidden, runs leading to a 0-decision and to a 1-decision both remain reachable. Step 2: Whenever the protocol nears committing, the scheduler delays the message that would tip it. Step 3: The run stays bivalent forever—termination is violated while agreement and validity hold.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Slow and crashed are indistinguishable here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That claim is exactly what FLP disproves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deterministic async protocols have no such round guarantee.

hard.prompt: During a network partition, nodes on side A suspect side B and vice versa, and both sides could try electing leaders. What is the core danger, and what prevents it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wall-clock comparison prevents divergent writes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: TCP retransmission prevents divergent writes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Split-brain: two leaders accepting conflicting writes; majority quorums prevent it by letting only the majority side act.

choices.label: D
choices.body: There is no danger because timeouts prove death.

hard.hint: Next step: count which side still holds a majority.
hard.explanation: Mutual suspicion is expected under partition; only quorum rules stop both sides from writing.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: 5 nodes split 3/2; both sides time out and suspect the other. Step 2: The 3-node side can still gather majorities and elect a leader; the 2-node side cannot. Step 3: Minority-side writes block instead of diverging—suspicion starts elections, majorities finish them.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Clocks do not arbitrate write authority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TCP cannot cross a partition at all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Timeouts only raise suspicion, which both sides hold symmetrically.

hard.prompt: Two operations have Lamport stamps 5 and 7. Can you conclude the first caused the second?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No—Lamport stamps carry no ordering information at all.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No—Lamport order is necessary but not sufficient for causality; the events may be concurrent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes—a smaller stamp always means causation.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Yes, provided both ran on the same node.

hard.hint: Next step: find the missing direction of the implication.
hard.explanation: Concurrent events still get ordered stamps, so stamp order alone cannot prove causation.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Node X ticks to 5 doing foo; node Y independently ticks to 7 doing bar, with no messages exchanged. Step 2: Stamps read 5 < 7, yet neither node knew of the other. Step 3: Calling foo a cause of bar would be false—causality needs vector-clock comparison.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They do preserve causal direction; only the reverse inference fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Concurrent events still receive ordered stamps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Same-node program order is the only case where local stamps imply order.

hard.prompt: Node A at clock 1 sends a message stamped 2. Node B's clock reads 5 when it arrives, then B performs one local event. What stamps do B's receive and local event carry?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Receive 5, then local event 5.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Receive 7, then local event 2.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Receive = max(5,2)+1 = 6; local event = 7.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Receive 2, then local event 3.

hard.hint: Next step: apply max-plus-one first, then increment.
hard.explanation: The receive merges histories to 6; the next local tick makes 7.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: B receives stamp 2 while local is 5, so max = 5. Step 2: Plus one gives the receive event stamp 6, exceeding both the send and B's prior state. Step 3: The following local event increments to 7, keeping B's sequence strictly increasing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Clocks must strictly increase along the causal chain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That inverts the order and skips the max-plus-one merge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That ignores B's own clock of 5 entirely.

hard.prompt: Two writes carry vectors [2,1,0] and [1,2,0]. A replica receives both. What must it do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Order them by wall-clock arrival time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Treat them as concurrent (incomparable) and invoke conflict handling—neither happened-before the other.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Treat [2,1,0] as causally later and drop the other.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Drop both writes as Byzantine attacks.

hard.hint: Next step: test the ≤ relation in both directions.
hard.explanation: First entry 2 > 1 but second entry 1 < 2, so neither vector dominates—concurrency.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Compare: entry one 2 > 1 favors the first write; entry two 1 < 2 favors the second. Step 2: Neither history contains the other, so last-writer-wins by vector is undefined. Step 3: The store must keep both versions (Dynamo-style siblings) or merge via CRDT rules and let the app reconcile.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Arrival order is not causal order; clocks skew.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The first entry leads but the second trails, so dominance fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Incomparability is normal concurrency, not evidence of malice.

hard.prompt: Two teams debate: team A says 'our RPC library gives exactly-once', team B says 'exactly-once is impossible'. How are both partly right?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Exactly-once delivery exists at the TCP layer alone.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Retried calls can never duplicate any effect.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Idempotence alone removes the need for request IDs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The network cannot prevent duplicates, but the visible effect can appear exactly-once when dedup plus idempotence bound the effect.

hard.hint: Next step: separate 'message delivered once' from 'effect applied once'.
hard.explanation: Impossibility applies to delivery; engineering achieves once-per-effect with state.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: request executes, ack is lost, client retries—two deliveries happened. Step 2: The server's dedup table maps id=7 to the first receipt and replays it. Step 3: The client observes one charge—delivery duplicated, effect did not.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TCP retransmits and connections break; apps still see duplicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Any retry after an ambiguous failure may re-execute.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Some operations have no natural idempotent form and need IDs.

hard.prompt: A 'refund payment P' handler checks 'if not refunded(P): refund(P)'. Under concurrent duplicate retries, a double refund still occurs. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Refunds are mathematically non-idempotent by nature.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The database is too slow to store flags.

choices.label: C
choices.body: TCP duplicated the packets on the wire.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The check-then-act is not atomic: two retries can both pass the check before either records the refund.

hard.hint: Next step: interleave two retries line by line.
hard.explanation: Idempotence logic must execute atomically with the effect, or races reintroduce duplicates.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: retry A checks refunded(P)=false; retry B checks refunded(P)=false. Step 2: Both issue the refund, then both set the flag—two payouts. Step 3: Fix with a unique constraint or atomic compare-and-set on the refund record.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: With an atomic dedup record, refund becomes idempotent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed is not the issue; atomicity of check plus act is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Duplicates are expected; the handler must tolerate them atomically.

hard.prompt: A client retries with identical request ID 3 times; the server executed attempt 1 but crashed before persisting the dedup record, then executes retry 2 fully. What went wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The client used the same request ID too often.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Three retries are always too many.

choices.label: C
choices.body: At-least-once delivery is impossible here.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The dedup record was not persisted atomically with the effect, so the crash erased the only memory of attempt 1.

hard.hint: Next step: check what survived the crash.
hard.explanation: Request IDs only help if stored durably in the same atomic step as the side effect.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Attempt 1 charges the card but the dedup write sits in a lost buffer. Step 2: Crash wipes the buffer; retry 2 finds no record and charges again. Step 3: Fix by committing effect plus dedup key in one transaction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Reusing the ID is correct; the server failed to honor it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Retry count is irrelevant when dedup state is lost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Delivery worked; the exactly-once effect failed for lack of atomic dedup.

hard.prompt: A dedup table keyed by request ID is sharded across servers, and retries may land on a different shard that has no record. What is the fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Store dedup records only in local memory per server.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Drop the request ID and rely on timestamps.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Route retries deterministically to the shard owning the ID (e.g., hash the ID), or share the dedup store.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use random load balancing for retries.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which server can see the original record.
hard.explanation: Dedup state must be reachable from wherever the retry lands.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Attempt 1 lands on shard S1, storing id=5. Step 2: Retry lands on S2 with no record and re-executes. Step 3: Hashing id=5 to S1 for all attempts—or a shared dedup table—closes the hole.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Local-only records are invisible to the retry's new owner.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Timestamps do not identify duplicates reliably.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random routing is what strands retries away from their records.

hard.prompt: Why must the dedup check and the side effect commit in one atomic step?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Atomicity only matters for read performance.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Separate steps are fine because crashes are rare.

choices.label: C
choices.body: TCP ordering already makes them atomic.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Otherwise a crash between them leaves the effect applied with no record, or a record with no effect, breaking exactly-once appearance.

hard.hint: Next step: crash the server between the two steps on paper.
hard.explanation: Two separate steps create a window where state and memory disagree.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Effect commits, crash, dedup row lost: retry double-applies. Step 2: Dedup row commits, crash, effect lost: retry returns a receipt for work never done. Step 3: One transaction for both keeps memory and reality in sync.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This is a correctness requirement, not a speed tweak.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rare crashes still corrupt payments; correctness must hold under failure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TCP orders bytes on one connection; it does not join DB writes.

hard.prompt: An engineer claims 'we use TCP, so our increment-counter RPC runs exactly once'. Give the concrete counterexample trace.

choices.label: A
choices.body: TCP merges two increments into one segment.

choices.label: B
choices.body: TCP acks prove the app processed the call.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Server increments, ack is lost on a broken connection, client retries on a new connection, server increments again: counter +2 for one intent.

choices.label: D
choices.body: TCP reorders the increment above the read.

hard.hint: Next step: draw the broken connection between execute and ack.
hard.explanation: Exactly-once needs app semantics; transport reliability is necessary but insufficient.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: INCR arrives over conn A; counter 5 -> 6. Step 2: Conn A breaks; ack never reaches the client. Step 3: Retry over conn B runs INCR again: 6 -> 7. One user click, two increments.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Segmentation does not change application execution count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TCP acks confirm byte receipt, not application processing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TCP preserves order; the issue is retry across connections.

hard.prompt: A gateway sheds load by failing fast, but a downstream BatchJob service holds each admitted call for 10 minutes. Why can the gateway still die?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Long calls use zero resources while waiting.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Backpressure is impossible with batch jobs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Admitted long-held calls pin threads and memory, so even a trickle of admissions accumulates into exhaustion.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Failing fast never sheds any load.

hard.hint: Next step: multiply held calls by minutes admitted per minute.
hard.explanation: Backpressure must bound holding time too, not just admission rate.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Gateway admits 10 batch calls/s, each held 600 s: 6000 held concurrently. Step 2: Threads and heap grow until GC thrash and OOM. Step 3: Fix with deadlines, async job polling, and cancellation of abandoned calls.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Each held call pins a thread, socket, and buffers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deadlines plus async polling bound even batch work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Failing fast sheds the rejected calls; the leak is the held ones.

hard.prompt: Service A (deadline 2 s) calls B, which fans out to C and D in parallel. C is slow. How should B handle its remaining budget?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Restart the full 2 s budget at each fan-out.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Return success without waiting for either.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Race C and D against the remaining budget, cancel stragglers, and return the best available result or a bounded error.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Wait for C indefinitely past A's deadline.

hard.hint: Next step: ask whose waiting the leftover budget protects.
hard.explanation: Hedging plus cancellation spends the shared budget wisely.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: B has 600 ms left when C stalls and D answers. Step 2: B cancels C, returns D's result within budget. Step 3: Optional hedging—send a second request to C's replica—further trims the tail.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Fresh budgets per hop multiply tail latency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fabricating success violates correctness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That breaks A's contract and wastes work nobody will read.

hard.prompt: A chat service streams messages with at-least-once redelivery after reconnects. Users see duplicate messages. What is the minimal correct fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deduplicate by message timestamp.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Attach per-message IDs; the client renders each ID once and advances its resume cursor only past contiguous IDs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Switch the stream to at-most-once.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Remove the resume cursor entirely.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what identifies 'already seen' across reconnects.
hard.explanation: Stream dedup mirrors RPC dedup: IDs plus a persisted cursor.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Reconnect replays msgs 98–102 already shown. Step 2: Client checks IDs, renders only unseen ones, and moves its cursor to 102. Step 3: The server resumes after 102—duplicates delivered, never displayed twice.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Timestamps collide and skew; IDs are exact.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: At-most-once would lose messages on every reconnect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Without a cursor every reconnect replays from scratch.

hard.prompt: A store claims linearizability but routes reads to any single replica with no version check. A write completes on a quorum, then a read hits a stale replica. What is the flaw?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Single-replica reads without contacting a quorum or the leader can miss the linearized write.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Quorum writes are unnecessary for linearizability.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stale reads are legal under linearizability.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Adding more replicas fixes the read path.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which replicas the read intersected with the write quorum.
hard.explanation: Linearizability needs overlap on reads too: quorum reads, leader reads, or version checks.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: W=3/5 write of v2 completes; read hits one of the 2 stale replicas. Step 2: Read and write sets never intersect, so v2 is invisible. Step 3: Fix with R+W>N reads, leader-lease reads, or read-index confirmation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Writes alone do not help if reads bypass them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A completed write must be visible to later reads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More replicas without a read protocol only add staleness.

hard.prompt: A system orders operations by Lamport timestamp alone and claims sequential consistency. Two causally unrelated writes get stamps 3 and 4; a process that issued stamp-4's write earlier in program order sees 3 applied first. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lamport order can contradict a process's program order, so timestamps alone do not yield a valid sequential order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Lamport timestamps always respect program order.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sequential consistency forbids concurrent writes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Vector clocks would make it linearizable.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether the global order kept each sender's own sequence.
hard.explanation: A valid sequential order must embed every program order; raw Lamport sort may not.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: P1 issues w1 then w2, but w2's Lamport stamp sorts before a concurrent w0. Step 2: Sorting purely by stamp can place w2 before w1 globally. Step 3: That inverts P1's program order—fix with a sequencer or per-process sequence enforcement.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Local ticks rise, but merging remote stamps can interleave badly without tie-breaking by process order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Concurrency is allowed; the violation is program-order inversion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Vector clocks give causality, not real-time linearizability.

hard.prompt: An eventually consistent counter uses naive read-then-write increments on two replicas during a partition; each side counts 5 clicks. After healing, the merged value reads 5 instead of 10. What went wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lost update: each side read the same base and wrote back absolute values, so one side's increments overwrote the other's.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The network duplicated the increments.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Eventual consistency forbids all counters.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Quorums were too large.

hard.hint: Next step: trace each side's read value and write-back.
hard.explanation: Read-modify-write without causality tracking loses concurrent updates.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Both sides read 0, count 5 locally, write back 5. Step 2: Merge picks one '5' (LWW or last arrived). Step 3: Five clicks vanish—fix with a grow-only counter CRDT or a strongly consistent increment.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Duplication would inflate the count, not halve it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Counters work with CRDT (G-Counter) or atomic increments, not naive read-write.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No quorum was used; each side wrote locally with no merge rule.

hard.prompt: N=5, W=2, R=2 (so W+R=4 ≤ 5). A write completes on {A,B}; a read hits {D,E}. What can the read return, and what is the lesson?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A Byzantine fault proof against A and B.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A stale value: non-overlapping quorums may miss the newest write entirely—this configuration cannot promise strong reads.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always the newest write, since W=2 is a quorum.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An automatic merge of all five replicas.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether the two sets share a member.
hard.explanation: Overlap is load-bearing: W+R ≤ N breaks the strong-read promise.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Write set {A,B}, read set {D,E}: disjoint. Step 2: The reader sees only pre-write versions and returns stale data legally under this config. Step 3: Fix by sizing R+W>N (or routing reads through the leader) before claiming strong consistency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This is quorum math, not malice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Without overlap, 'quorum' alone guarantees nothing about visibility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No merge runs; the read simply sees whoever it contacted.

hard.prompt: Two replicas hold a PN-Counter (increment and decrement CRDT). Replica A applied +3/-1 locally, replica B applied +2/-2 locally, then they sync. What is the merged value, and why is it exact?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 2: per-replica increment and decrement tallies merge by max (5 ups, 3 downs), then value = 5 − 3 = 2.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 0, because concurrent updates cancel out.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 6, summing all absolute values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It depends on which replica syncs first.

hard.hint: Next step: split each side into P (ups) and N (downs) vectors.
hard.explanation: Grow-only parts merge by max, giving an exact total regardless of order.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Increment tallies [A:3, B:2] merge entry-wise by max: total ups = 3 + 2 = 5. Step 2: Decrement tallies [A:1, B:2] merge the same way: total downs = 1 + 2 = 3. Step 3: Value = 5 − 3 = 2 on every replica: no update lost or double-counted, in any sync order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Opposite operations on different replicas do not cancel; both count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Decrements subtract; they do not add.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Max-merges are order-independent by construction.

hard.prompt: When should you NOT reach for a CRDT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When availability matters more than immediacy.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When operations need global invariants (e.g., 'balance never negative' or unique usernames)—CRDTs converge state but cannot prevent concurrent violations.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When replicas may be partitioned.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When updates are commutative.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what two concurrent legal-everywhere updates could jointly break.
hard.explanation: Convergence without coordination cannot enforce a global predicate.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Balance 10; A withdraws 10, B withdraws 10 concurrently—each locally legal. Step 2: Merged state shows −10: converged but invalid. Step 3: Invariants like uniqueness or non-negativity need consensus or conditional writes, not merge rules.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That tradeoff favors CRDTs, not against them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Partitions are exactly where CRDTs shine.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Commutative updates are the ideal CRDT case.

hard.prompt: A cluster relies ONLY on read-repair (no anti-entropy). A rarely-read key loses its newest version on the one replica holding it when that disk dies. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The loss is impossible with quorum writes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The update is lost: no live replica and no background copy noticed, and future reads cannot resurrect what nobody holds.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Read-repair resurrects it from checksums.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gossip recreates the value from thin air.

hard.hint: Next step: count the surviving copies of that key's newest version.
hard.explanation: Read-repair heals divergence; only background replication plus durable quorums preserve endangered copies.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: v9 existed only on disk D (other replicas never got it or were repaired backward). Step 2: D dies before any read observes v9 elsewhere. Step 3: v9 is gone—hinted handoff, proper W sizing, and anti-entropy exist to prevent single-copy windows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Quorum writes spread copies, but without repair the last copy can still die.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Checksums detect corruption; they do not store the value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Gossip copies existing state; extinct data stays extinct.

hard.prompt: A photo app promises read-your-writes. A user uploads a photo (acked on replica A), then immediately lists photos via replica B and the photo is missing. Which implementation gap caused this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The list request was not routed with the session's causality: it read from B without waiting for A's version.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eventual consistency makes this impossible to fix.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The upload must have failed silently.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Linearizability is the only possible fix.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what version information traveled with the list request.
hard.explanation: Session guarantees ride on propagating the client's last-write version to its reads.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Upload returns version 12 from A. Step 2: The list request carries no '≥12' requirement and lands on B at version 10. Step 3: Fix: pin the session to A, or make B block until version 12 arrives (writes-follow-reads generalized).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Session stickiness or version-gating fixes it without global strength.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The ack proves the write landed; the read simply missed it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Per-session guarantees are far cheaper than global linearizability.

hard.prompt: Causal consistency requires: if operation A happened-before B, every node observes A before B. Two users post concurrently with no causal link. What ordering does causal consistency require between them?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both posts must be rejected.

choices.label: B
choices.body: None—concurrent operations may appear in different orders on different nodes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All nodes must agree on one order for them.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The later wall-clock post must appear first.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether a happened-before edge exists.
hard.explanation: Causality constrains only dependent operations; independent ones float.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Alice posts P, Bob posts Q, neither saw the other—no causal path. Step 2: Node 1 shows P then Q; node 2 shows Q then P. Step 3: Both views respect all happened-before edges (there are none between P and Q)—causally consistent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Concurrency is legal; only causal chains are ordered.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Total agreement on concurrent ops is sequential/linearizable strength.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Wall clocks do not define causality.

hard.prompt: Two proposers duel: P1 with ballot 5, P2 with ballot 6, alternating prepares so neither finishes. What breaks the livelock, and what safety still holds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Safety is violated until one wins.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Acceptors must forget all promises to recover.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ballots must decrease to resolve contention.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Randomized backoff or a stable leader lets one ballot complete; safety (at most one chosen value) held throughout the duel.

hard.hint: Next step: separate liveness (stuck) from safety (wrong value).
hard.explanation: Paxos is safe under contention; liveness needs one proposer to outlast the other.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Trace: P1 prepare(5) promised; P2 prepare(6) overrides; P1 retries prepare(7), overriding back. Step 2: No accept quorum ever forms, so nothing is chosen—safe but stalled. Step 3: Electing P2 sole proposer (or backoff) lets ballot 6 run prepare then accept to completion.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Dueling delays termination but never allows two chosen values.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Forgetting promises would break safety; they persist and rise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ballots rise monotonically; higher numbers win.

hard.prompt: Proposer P gets promises for ballot 9 from a majority; one reports accepted (7, Y). P prefers value Z. What must P send in its accept phase, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: accept(9, Z), since 9 outranks 7.

choices.label: B
choices.body: accept(7, Z) to overwrite history.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Nothing—ballot 9 is unusable after a report.

choices.label: D
choices.body: accept(9, Y): P must re-propose the highest reported accepted value, not its preferred Z.

hard.hint: Next step: ask whether Y might already have been chosen.
hard.explanation: The report rule converts 'maybe chosen' into 'definitely preserved'.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: (7,Y) may have reached a majority without P knowing. Step 2: If P proposed Z at ballot 9 and won, two values would be chosen—safety violated. Step 3: Proposing Y at 9 keeps all futures consistent with the possible earlier choice.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Higher ballot wins the round but must carry forward the earlier value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Lower ballots cannot overwrite; promises already block them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The ballot is fine; only the value is constrained.

hard.prompt: An engineer claims 'Raft always elects the candidate with the most-up-to-date log'. What is wrong with 'always'?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Up-to-date-ness restricts who followers may vote for, but staggered timeouts and partitions decide who actually campaigns and wins among eligible candidates.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Raft has no log up-to-date check at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The most-up-to-date node is forbidden from campaigning.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Terms override log checks completely.

hard.hint: Next step: separate vote eligibility from election victory.
hard.explanation: Eligibility is necessary, not sufficient, for winning.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Nodes B and C both have full logs; A lags. Step 2: A's requests are denied by log checks, but B and C race—whoever times out first usually wins. Step 3: Either B or C becomes leader; 'most up-to-date' narrowed the field but did not pick the winner.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Voters do reject candidates with staler logs—that part is real.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: It may campaign; it is not guaranteed to win every race.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both apply: voters check term first, then log freshness.

hard.prompt: Leader L1 (term 2) partially replicates entry E to 2 of 5 nodes, then deposes. Leader L2 (term 3) overwrites E with E' on those nodes without E ever being committed. Is this legal in Raft?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes—uncommitted entries may be overwritten by a new leader; only committed entries are protected.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No—leaders may never overwrite any entry.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No—terms forbid all log changes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Yes, and committed entries may be overwritten too.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether E reached a majority.
hard.explanation: Two copies are not a commit; the new leader's log governs.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: E sits on 2/5 nodes—no majority, uncommitted. Step 2: L2's AppendEntries with higher term forces followers to match its log, erasing E. Step 3: No client was ever acked for E, so no durability promise breaks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Overwrite freedom for uncommitted suffixes is how Raft converges.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Higher-term leaders routinely repair conflicting suffixes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Committed entries are inviolable; only uncommitted ones yield.

hard.prompt: A follower's log is longer than the leader's but contains uncommitted suffix entries the leader lacks. How do the logs converge?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The follower votes itself leader to protect its suffix.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The follower deletes its conflicting suffix and copies the leader's entries from the first divergence point.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The leader adopts the follower's longer suffix.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both logs keep their own suffixes forever.

hard.hint: Next step: find the last index where the two logs agree.
hard.explanation: The leader forces followers' logs to match its own—Leader Completeness plus Log Matching.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Leader log ends at index 6; follower has extra uncommitted 7–9 from an old term. Step 2: AppendEntries consistency checks fail at 7; the leader decrements nextIndex. Step 3: At the divergence point the follower truncates 7–9 and replicates the leader's suffix.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Higher-term leadership, not log length, decides authority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Authority flows leader-to-follower only; the leader never copies followers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Divergence would fork the state machine.

hard.prompt: Why can terms in Raft skip (e.g., jump from 3 to 6) yet safety still holds?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Failed elections increment terms without winners, so gaps are harmless; monotonicity, not contiguity, is what safety needs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Skipped terms secretly elect hidden leaders.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gaps mean committed entries were lost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Terms must be contiguous for voting to work.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what elected anyone in terms 4 and 5.
hard.explanation: Nobody won those terms—candidates just incremented and failed.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Candidates for terms 4 and 5 split votes and time out. Step 2: Term 6's candidate finally gathers a majority. Step 3: Safety uses term ordering (higher supersedes lower), which gaps preserve.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No leader exists without majority votes in that term.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Commitment is term-independent once majority-stored.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Voters compare greater/less, never adjacency.

hard.prompt: Two candidates start term 7 nearly simultaneously. Each gets 2 of 5 votes plus its own (3 total each is impossible—say each holds 2 including self, one node abstains). What resolves this without violating safety?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The abstaining node picks both as leaders.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Neither wins; timeouts advance to term 8 where jitter lets one candidate gather a true majority.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both become co-leaders of term 7.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The term is decremented to 6 for a revote.

hard.hint: Next step: count whether anyone holds 3 of 5.
hard.explanation: Split votes preserve safety (no leader) while liveness retries in a new term.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Votes split 2-2 with one node unheard—no majority. Step 2: Term 7 expires leaderless; that is safe but stalled. Step 3: Randomized timeouts make a term-8 race decisive: one candidate collects 3+ votes and leads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One vote per term per node; double votes are illegal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two leaders per term would fork the log—forbidden.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Terms never decrease.

hard.prompt: An engineer proposes 4-node clusters as 'safer than 3-node'. What is the flaw?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 3-node clusters tolerate 2 failures.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 4 nodes still tolerate only 1 failure for majority (need 3), so fault tolerance matches 3 nodes while costing an extra server.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4-node clusters tolerate 3 failures.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Even-sized clusters cannot run Raft at all.

hard.hint: Next step: compute floor(4/2)+1 and failures survivable.
hard.explanation: Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance—prefer 3 or 5.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 4 nodes need 3 for majority: survives 1 failure. Step 2: 3 nodes need 2 for majority: also survives 1 failure. Step 3: The 4th server adds money and latency with zero extra resilience—use 5 to tolerate 2.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 3 nodes need 2 for majority, tolerating exactly 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Losing 2 of 4 leaves 2 < 3: no majority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: They run fine; they are just capacity-inefficient.

hard.prompt: For linearizable reads, why can't a Raft leader simply answer from its local state machine?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Read-index exchanges are pure overhead with no purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It might be a deposed leader: without confirming it still holds a majority (read-index or lease), its state could be stale.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Local reads are always linearizable in Raft.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Followers never have fresher state than leaders.

hard.hint: Next step: put the leader alone on one side of a partition.
hard.explanation: Leadership must be re-confirmed before trusting local state.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Leader L (term 4) partitions with 1 of 5 nodes; the other 4 elect term 5 and commit write W. Step 2: L's state lacks W but L does not know it is deposed. Step 3: Serving locally returns pre-W data—stale. Read-index (majority heartbeat round) or a lease exposes the deposition first.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They verify current leadership before serving the read.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A partitioned old leader's log stops advancing while clients moved on.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The leader could be the stale one during a partition.

hard.prompt: Three-phase commit (3PC) adds a pre-commit phase so participants know what before committing?

choices.label: A
choices.body: That all participants voted YES and will commit if the coordinator proceeds, enabling timeout-based recovery rules.

choices.label: B
choices.body: That no participant ever persisted any vote.

choices.label: C
choices.body: That any single lost byte forces abort.

choices.label: D
choices.body: That only one phase is needed in total.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what a participant in pre-commit can assume about the others.
hard.explanation: Shared knowledge of unanimity lets timeouts decide safely—except under partitions.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: All vote YES, then all acknowledge pre-commit: everyone knows everyone is ready. Step 2: A participant timing out in pre-commit may commit, knowing no one will abort. Step 3: But under network partition this reasoning fails—3PC still blocks or diverges there, so it is not a general async solution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Votes and states are still recorded durably.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 3PC does not abort on arbitrary loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 3PC has more phases: can-commit, pre-commit, commit.

hard.prompt: Why do sagas offer only semantic atomicity rather than true ACID atomicity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Intermediate steps commit and become visible before the saga finishes, so concurrent readers can observe partial outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sagas never commit any step until the end.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Compensations run before forward steps.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sagas hold global locks throughout.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what a concurrent reader sees mid-saga.
hard.explanation: Isolation is sacrificed; application design must tolerate transient partial states.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Saga creates order (visible), charges card (visible), then shipping fails. Step 2: Between steps 2 and 3, dashboards show a paid-but-unshipped order. Step 3: Compensation voids the charge, converging to 'nothing happened'—but observers briefly saw something.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Each step commits locally as it runs—that is the point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Compensations run only after a later failure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No global locks are held; that is why partial states show.

hard.prompt: Why is 'CAP means pick two of three, once and forever' a misconception?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Partitions are the only forced tradeoff; during normal operation the real tradeoff is latency vs consistency (PACELC), tunable per request.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Partitions never happen in practice.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Consistency and availability never conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Latency is unrelated to replication choices.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what the system trades when no partition exists.
hard.explanation: CAP constrains failures; PACELC's 'else' clause governs the common case.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Healthy network, W=ALL writes: consistent but slow. Step 2: Same network, W=1 writes: fast but briefly divergent. Step 3: Both run without partitions—the choice is latency vs consistency per operation, not a one-time 'pick two'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Partitions do happen; the point is they are intermittent, not permanent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Under partition they genuinely conflict.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sync replication buys consistency with latency every day.

hard.prompt: Dynamo-style AP systems under partition favor availability by offering what, and what is the cost?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Single-node two-phase locking only.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eventual consistency with conflict resolution (version vectors, LWW); the cost is temporary divergence callers must handle.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Strict serializability on every read without exception.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No writes allowed during normal operation.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what 'always writable' implies for concurrent writes.
hard.explanation: Accepting writes on both sides guarantees siblings that need merging.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Partition: both sides accept cart updates. Step 2: Heal: version vectors show concurrent siblings. Step 3: LWW or app merge converges—available throughout, consistent only after repair.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That ignores partition-first distributed design.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the CP choice under partition stress.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: AP systems keep accepting writes with later reconciliation.

hard.prompt: A team tunes W=ALL/R=1 for 'strong consistency with fast reads'. Under a single slow replica, what breaks first and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Partitions become impossible.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Write latency (and availability): every write waits for the slowest replica, and one failure blocks all writes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reads become linearizable for free.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing—W=ALL is always optimal.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which operation waits for the straggler.
hard.explanation: W=ALL couples every write to the slowest (or dead) replica.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 5 replicas, one disk stalls: each write waits on all 5. Step 2: p99 write latency tracks the straggler; if it dies, writes halt. Step 3: QUORUM writes (W=3) would mask one straggler—same healthy network, better latency point.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Replication factors do not prevent partitions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: R=1 reads can miss the newest write on a stale replica... actually W=ALL covers all, but a down node blocks writes first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: W=ALL maximizes write latency and minimizes write availability.

hard.prompt: Secondary indexes on a sharded table are hard because a lookup by non-key attribute may require what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Disabling all writes globally forever.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fitting the database in CPU cache.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Scatter-gather across many shards, or maintaining separate index partitions that must stay consistent.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only local disk access on one machine.

hard.hint: Next step: ask where the index entry for a key lives versus the row.
hard.explanation: Index placement and row placement follow different keys.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Row for user:42 lives on shard(hash(42)); email index entry lives on shard(hash(email)). Step 2: 'Find by email' fans out or hops twice. Step 3: Global secondary indexes replicate this cost on writes—every write updates row plus index shards.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Indexes are maintained during writes at extra cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scale-out systems never fit in cache.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Distributed index entries span shard boundaries.

hard.prompt: Elle finds a cycle in the observed transaction history (T1 read x written by T2, T2 read y written by T1, with real-time order violated). What does the cycle prove?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Serializability held with a hidden order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The execution was not serializable: no serial order of T1 and T2 explains all observations.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The network was merely slow.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The clients used weak passwords.

hard.hint: Next step: try ordering T1 before T2, then T2 before T1.
hard.explanation: Each order explains one dependency and breaks the other—no order works.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: T1-before-T2 explains T2's read of y but contradicts T1 reading T2's x first. Step 2: T2-before-T1 fails symmetrically. Step 3: The history is unserializable; the DB's isolation claim is refuted for this run.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A cycle means every candidate serial order contradicts some observation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Slowness alone cannot create dependency cycles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Authentication is irrelevant to isolation cycles.

hard.prompt: A vendor dismisses a Jepsen finding as 'only under partition, which never happens'. What is the correct response?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Demand zero faults instead of handling them.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Blame the test harness for finding the bug.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Partitions do happen (and Jepsen models routine faults); a claimed guarantee must hold in its stated failure model or the claim must shrink.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Accept the dismissal and ship without changes.

hard.hint: Next step: ask what failure model the marketing claim assumed.
hard.explanation: Guarantees are scoped to a model—test inside that scope.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Vendor claims 'linearizable under partition'. Step 2: Jepsen partitions and observes stale reads. Step 3: Either fix the protocol or narrow the claim (e.g., 'linearizable only without partitions')—dismissing the fault concedes nothing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Faults are inevitable; design for the stated model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The checker reports histories; the system produced them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Untested fault paths become outage paths.

hard.prompt: Distributed strict 2PL across shards can block indefinitely when the coordinator fails mid-commit. What architectural fix removes the blocking without losing atomicity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Remove all locks and hope for the best.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replicate the transaction decision through consensus (Paxos-commit / replicated coordinator state) so recovery always finds the outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hold shard locks forever until an operator intervenes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Let each shard decide commit/abort independently.

hard.hint: Next step: ask where the single copy of 'the decision' lives.
hard.explanation: One fault-tolerant decision record turns blocking 2PC/2PL into recoverable commit.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Coordinator replicates COMMIT to a Raft group before replying. Step 2: Coordinator crashes; a shard queries the replicated log and finds COMMIT. Step 3: All shards converge to commit—atomicity holds, nobody blocks on one dead box.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hopeless concurrency corrupts isolation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Manual recovery is the outage, not the fix.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Independent decisions fork atomicity—some commit, some abort.
